basis: New mission, no workbook source. Facts: Taiwan annual rainfall ~2,500mm, ~2.5x world average, but usable water per capita only ~4,074 m3/yr (~1/5 world average) (Water Resources Agency, MOEA). ~80% of rain falls May-Oct; typhoons + summer plum rains supply >50% of annual water; 2021 was the first year since 1964/56 years with no typhoon landfall, triggering the worst drought in decades (WRA; Earth.org; NPR/KPBS Apr 2023). Deji Reservoir sedimentation ~47% of capacity lost (WRA data, widely reported). 2021 drought: 17 of 19 major reservoirs <50%, Baoshan No.2 ~7%, Techi ~4.4%, rationing 2 days/week for >1 million households ~2 months (Earth.org; NPR). National reservoir dredging has exceeded average annual sediment inflow since 2022 (WRA); Shihmen Amuping Desilting Tunnel operating since Sept 2023 (WRA). Hsinchu desalination plant ~13,000 tonnes/day; national pipe leakage fell from ~20% a decade ago to ~14% now (Earth.org). Water price ~NT$11/tonne, several times cheaper than US/UK (Earth.org). Agriculture uses >70% of Taiwan's water but <2% of GDP (Earth.org; multiple sources). Register per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md.

slides.1: Taiwan has a strange water problem. In some years, we must save every drop. In other years, heavy rain causes terrible floods. Why does this happen to us?
slides.2: SDG 6 means clean water and toilets for everyone. It is not only about having enough water. The water must also be safe and fair for all people.
slides.3: Each year, Taiwan gets a huge amount of rain — about 2,500mm. That is 2.5 times the world average. But each person can only use a fifth of that amount.
slides.4: Taiwan's mountains are steep, and its rivers are short. So rain runs fast into the sea. Most rain falls between May and October, so the rest of the year is dry.
slides.5: Typhoons and summer rain give us over half of our yearly water. In 2021, no typhoon came for the first time in 56 years. A bad drought soon followed.
slides.6: Every year, mud slowly fills up our reservoirs. Deji Reservoir has already lost about 47% of its space this way. A full reservoir on paper may still be empty underwater.
slides.7: In 2021, 17 of 19 big reservoirs fell below half full. Baoshan No. 2 dropped to 7%, and Techi to 4.4%. Water was cut for over a million homes.
slides.8: Since 2022, workers have removed more mud than flows in each year. The Shihmen tunnel has run since September 2023. It clears mud and also stops floods.
slides.9: A new plant in Hsinchu now makes 13,000 tonnes of water a day. Old pipes also leak less water now, down from 20% to about 14%.
slides.10: Taiwan cannot use reservoirs alone anymore. New pipes now move water between regions in a dry year. We also make water from the sea and from used water.
slides.11: New treatment plants are not enough on their own. Old pipes must be fixed too, or we lose water we already cleaned. We should not waste what we have.
slides.12: Water here costs only NT$11 for one tonne. That is far cheaper than in the US or the UK. A higher price could stop waste, but poor families would suffer.
slides.13: Climate change now hits our typhoons. Experts say big storms will not come as often. Our reservoirs need rain every single year to stay full.
slides.14: But when a typhoon comes now, the rain falls too fast and hard. Reservoirs cannot hold it all, so floods happen instead. More rain does not fix our problem.
slides.15: When a drought hits, farmers must leave fields empty first. This saves water for cities and factories. Farms use over 70% of our water but make under 2% of our GDP.
slides.16: This is not only about money. In 2021, many families and students had no water for two whole months. That was real life, not just numbers on a page.
slides.17: To sum up, Taiwan gets huge rain but very little water we can use. A hotter climate is making this gap even harder to close.
slides.18: This is not really about people wasting water. Land shape, old pipes and climate add up together. Blaming only daily habits misses the real cause.
slides.19: So what can you do? Study the water data that the government shares online. Support better pipes and fair prices, or study engineering to help fix this.
slides.20: Taiwan needs fresh ideas for a drier future. Let's not just wait and hope for rain. Let's use our skills to build a smarter water system for everyone.
